title: Concept Drills — Introduction to Biology (Class 11 Biology)
subject: biology

questions.question: A car moves, uses fuel and responds to the road. Why is it not alive? Name the criterion that separates it from living things.
questions.solution: The missing criteria: self-reproduction with heredity, growth from within (metabolism-driven, not assembly), cellular organisation, and response/adaptation through evolution. A car's motion comes from an external design and fuel burn, not internal metabolism; it cannot replicate or evolve. Metabolism + reproduction + evolution are the decisive markers.

questions.question: Why does the study of biology need multiple levels (molecule → cell → tissue → organism → ecosystem) rather than one?
questions.solution: Each level has EMERGENT properties not predictable from the level below: a heart's pumping is not obvious from muscle chemistry; an ecosystem's stability is not obvious from individual organisms. Different questions live at different levels — enzyme mechanism vs population dynamics. Reductionism explains parts; holism explains wholes.

questions.question: Testing a new fertiliser, why must one plot receive NO fertiliser at all?
questions.solution: The control plot shows what happens WITHOUT the treatment — baseline growth from soil, water, weather. Without it, you cannot attribute the treated plot's extra growth to the fertiliser rather than to conditions. A control isolates the variable being tested; it is the comparison that makes the conclusion valid.

questions.concept: Branches of biology and their overlap
questions.question: Why can't biology be neatly split into botany and zoology anymore?
questions.solution: Modern biology cuts across organisms: molecular biology, genetics, biotechnology and ecology use the same principles from bacteria to whales. DNA, energy flow and evolution are universal — a gene works similarly in plant and animal. The discipline is now organised by PROCESS (genetics, ecology, physiology) more than by organism group.

questions.question: Give two concrete examples where biological knowledge directly solves a human problem.
questions.solution: (1) Medicine: understanding microbes and immunity produced vaccines and antibiotics — smallpox eliminated by biological knowledge. (2) Agriculture: understanding genetics and plant physiology produced high-yield, disease-resistant crops (Green Revolution, Bt cotton). Biology's applications run from health to food security to environment.

questions.concept: Why biology is a science of comparisons
questions.question: Why does a single observation rarely establish a biological claim, while repeated controlled comparison does?
questions.solution: Living systems vary: individuals differ genetically and environmentally, so a single case cannot separate the factor of interest from natural variation. Controlled comparison with replication and a control group isolates the variable by averaging out the noise. Biology's subject matter is variable by nature, so inference must be statistical.

questions.concept: Why a hypothesis must be falsifiable
questions.question: A claim that 'all organisms have an invisible life force' cannot be tested. Why is unfalsifiability a defect in a scientific hypothesis?
questions.solution: If no conceivable observation could contradict a claim, then no evidence can support it either — it makes no prediction to check. Science advances by eliminating wrong hypotheses, which requires them to be refutable. Falsifiability is what makes a claim empirical rather than merely stated.

questions.concept: Why taxonomy reflects relationship not convenience
questions.question: Modern classification groups crocodiles with birds rather than with lizards. Why does classification follow ancestry rather than appearance?
questions.solution: Appearance converges: similar environments produce similar forms (analogy) without shared ancestry. Classification aims to represent evolutionary relationship (homology), so groups must be monophyletic — sharing an exclusive common ancestor. Crocodiles and birds share a more recent ancestor than crocodiles and lizards. Classification is a genealogy, not a catalogue of looks.
